description: "An interactive proof that every omega-word decomposes as a finite prefix followed by infinitely many interchangeable repeating blocks."
---

```{=html}
<div class="proof-lab" data-proof-lab="ramsey-decomposition"></div>
<noscript>
  <h1>Ramsey decomposition</h1>
  <p><strong>Theorem.</strong> Every omega-word alpha belongs to U&middot;V-omega for
  some classes U, V of a finite-index congruence (=), with V&middot;V contained in V.</p>

  <p><strong>Running example.</strong> The automaton has states s0, s1, s2 with
  F = {s1} and transitions s0-a-&gt;s1, s1-b-&gt;s2, s2-c-&gt;s2 (self-loop),
  s2-a-&gt;s1. The word alpha = abc&middot;abcc&middot;abccc&middot;&middot;&middot; has
  ever-growing gaps of c's and is not ultimately periodic, yet every block abc^n
  produces the same behaviour, so alpha decomposes as [epsilon]&middot;V-omega for a
  single class V.</p>

  <p><strong>Strategy.</strong> Build a second finite-index equivalence on the
  positions of alpha by colouring each pair of positions with the (=)-class of the
  segment between them. Pigeonhole gives an infinite pairwise-merging set of
  positions; persistence (congruence applied to a shared future suffix) makes that
  merge survive forever. A separate pigeonhole on cumulative-prefix classes gives
  infinitely many prefixes in one class V; persistence then transfers V's class onto
  each gap, turning them into genuine consecutive V-blocks. One witnessed
  concatenation transports, via congruence, to V&middot;V contained in V.</p>

  <p><strong>Proof outline.</strong></p>
  <ol>
    <li><em>Setup.</em> The congruence (=) compares the finite segments between
    positions, not positions themselves; so build a relation on positions, colouring
    a pair (k, k') by the (=)-class of the shared-future segments alpha(k, m) and
    alpha(k', m).</li>
    <li><em>Pigeonhole on positions.</em> That relation inherits finite index from
    (=), so among any r+1 positions two must merge; run over all of N to get an
    infinite pairwise-merging sequence k0 &lt; k1 &lt; k2 &lt; ...</li>
    <li><em>Persistence.</em> (=) is right-invariant, so appending the shared suffix
    to both sides shows: once two positions merge at some checkpoint m, they merge at
    every later checkpoint m' &gt;= m.</li>
    <li><em>Pigeonhole on segments.</em> Independently, pigeonhole the cumulative
    prefixes alpha(k0, ki): infinitely many share one class V. This gives alpha in
    U&middot;(infinitely many V-prefixes), but not yet consecutive blocks.</li>
    <li><em>Thinning.</em> Thin the sequence so that k0, ..., ki all merge at k(i+1);
    persistence transfers alpha(k0, k(i+1)) in V onto the gap, giving alpha(ki, k(i+1))
    in V. Every consecutive block lies in V, so alpha in U&middot;V-omega.</li>
    <li><em>Idempotence.</em> For one witnessed pair a = alpha(k0, k1), b =
    alpha(k1, k2) with ab in V, congruence gives xy = ab in V for all x = a, y = b in
    V; hence V&middot;V contained in V.</li>
  </ol>

  <p><strong>Conclusion.</strong> alpha in U&middot;V-omega with V&middot;V contained
  in V &mdash; the Ramsey decomposition, holding even when alpha is not ultimately
  periodic.</p>
</noscript>
```
